title: An Innovative American School: Black Mountain College

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Of the American 'progressive' colleges founded in the early 20th century, Black Mountain College was among the most distinctive, with an emphasis on its arts program. Black Mountain was established in 1933 on rented property in the mountains of North Carolina, and lasted only until 1957. Its founding faculty, the teaching staff, were eager to apply philosopher John Dewey’s 'learn by doing' principles to higher education. Dewey himself visited the college in 1935 and approved of what he saw.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The student population of Black Mountain was quite small, averaging no more than 40 students. Faculty and students lived and worked close together, and made decisions by achieving a consensus within the group. Yet, small as it was, few American schools have attracted such sustained attention, due largely to the many important artists who worked there. Major 20th-century figures such as painters Willem de Kooning and Robert Motherwell, composer John Cage and dance choreographer Merce Cunningham were among its teachers.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Black Mountain's imaginative curriculum was always centered around its arts program, run by the German immigrant artist Josef Albers, a former master teacher at Bauhaus, an innovative design academy in Germany. He primarily taught the nature of artistic illusion, challenging students to explore the relativity of color – how colors and materials can be made to change their appearance. For example, he considered it a good trick when shown an artwork in which marbles were made to look like fish eggs, or a brick resembled a loaf of bread.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Photographs of Albers teaching make him resemble a kindergarten teacher – down on his knees adjusting colored paper, or guiding a student's hand in a drawing class – rather than a traditional lecturer. And Albers seems to have inspired other teachers at the college to teach in similar experience-based ways, not only in the arts but in other subjects, such as mathematics and biology.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The college had no grades, no required courses, and no standard exams. The painter Jack Tworkov reported, 'People study what they please, as long as they want to, graduate whenever they are willing to stand on examination ... They can attend classes, or stay away. They can work entirely by themselves, or they need not work whatever ... Yet, much work is being done here.' Black Mountain was innovative in other ways, too. It was the first southern US college to enroll an African-American at a time when white and black Americans were segregated. Also, Albers invited the African-American painter Jacob Lawrence to teach at Black Mountain. While there, Lawrence painted Watchmaker, a painting that used unexpected color combinations, carried over from Albers' teachings.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In 1937, the college left its original campus. When a design for a new complex by Bauhaus architects proved too expensive to build, students and faculty took on the work of building a new school themselves. For four years, they held classes at one facility and then, in the afternoon, loaded up a truck and drove to the future campus to construct new buildings. Some of that mobility and can-do attitude can be seen in the work of Black Mountain art students: Ruth Asawa's hanging wire sculptures, inspired by the Mexican tradition of basketry, have a swaying, lifelike quality, while Robert Rauschenberg's odd 'portable room' is made to look like walls covered with rubbish, using paper, fabric, wood, paint and other materials. It looks like something a student might make after a day of hammering nails, and driving the trash truck - Rauschenberg's campus employment.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Theater Piece No. 1, from 1952, is perhaps the best-known event in the history of the college, and today is regarded as the first 'happening' – a rule-breaking artistic performance involving simultaneous, unrelated and partially improvised activities. Happenings became a well-known art form in the 1960s, helping to shape the now established genre of performance art. John Cage conceived the broad idea for the performance one morning, and by evening had persuaded other faculty and students to participate. Cage mounted a stepladder and spoke about music and philosophy while a movie was shown, dogs barked, a piano was played, and whistles blew.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Theater Piece No. 1 prompted later notable collaborations. In 1953, Cunningham founded his dance company at the college, before moving it to New York City. The previous year, composer Cage had performed his piece 4'33", in which a pianist sits at a piano for exactly four minutes and thirty-three seconds of silence. In New York, Cage, choreographer Cunningham, and Rauschenberg collaborated on performances. First, each would work separately to develop his own concept – for dance, music, sets, and costumes. Then later, these were assembled, as in Theater Piece No. 1, just as the actual performance was about to start.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: In recent decades, there have been several exhibitions devoted to the legacy of Black Mountain College, in the US and internationally, including shows in France, Spain and Germany. Also, in 2016, the Institute of Contemporary Art in Boston staged an ambitious exhibition devoted to this small North Carolina college that had closed almost sixty years before. At that closing, its final president, the poet Charles Olson, had observed simply, 'Why shouldn't things stop when they're over?'
